extracted.intended_audience: graduate or advanced undergraduate students studying probability theory and martingales
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter excerpt giving definitions, theorems, examples, and exercises about martingales: Doob inequalities, Lp convergence, square-integrable martingales, uniform integrability, backward martingales, and related probabilistic results (Borel-Cantelli, Radon–Nikodym application, de Finetti, Hewitt–Savage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Example: bounded sup but infinitely often values
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist processes with sup_n |X_n| < ∞ and P(X_n = a i.o.) = 1 for a = −1,0,1 showing that sup |X_{n+1}-X_n| < ∞ alone is not enough for the conclusion of Theorem 4.3.1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an illustrative counterexample (fine-tunable in Exercise 4.3.2) demonstrating that a martingale can converge in distribution without converging a.s. or in probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise 4.3.3: convergence under controlled conditional increment
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_n and Y_n are positive integrable and adapted to F_n, and E(X_{n+1}|F_n) ≤ X_n + Y_n with Σ Y_m < ∞ a.s., then X_n converges a.s. to a finite limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: use the stopping time N = inf{k : Σ_{m=1}^k Y_m > M} and consider the stopped process to obtain a supermartingale at time N.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borel-Cantelli product equivalence (Exercise 4.3.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For p_m ∈ [0,1), ∏_{m=1}^∞ (1 − p_m) = 0 if and only if Σ_{m=1}^∞ p_m = ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Borel–Cantelli lemmas (classical equivalence between divergence of sums and vanishing product).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional Borel-Cantelli variant (Exercise 4.3.5)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the conditional version: divergence of conditional probabilities implies almost sure occurrence infinitely often.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martingale from Radon–Nikodym construction (Exercises 4.3.6–4.3.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example 4.3.7 produces a martingale whose application of Theorem 4.3.5 yields a probabilistic proof: if F is countably generated and μ, ν are σ-finite with μ ≪ ν, then there is g with μ(A) = ∫_A g dν.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: conditional expectations needed have elementary definitions; this shows how martingale techniques can recover Radon–Nikodym.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bernoulli product measures criterion (Exercise 4.3.8(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: For product measures with factor probabilities α_n, β_n on {0,1}, Theorem 4.3.8 gives a necessary and sufficient condition for μ ≪ ν (absolute continuity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exercise asks to derive the explicit condition from Theorem 4.3.8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Square-sum criterion under bounded factors (Exercise 4.3.8(ii))
rubrics_metrics.description: If 0 < c ≤ α_n, β_n ≤ 1 − c < 1 for all n, then μ ≪ ν iff Σ (α_n − β_n)^2 < ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a concrete ℓ^2 condition when the Bernoulli parameters are bounded away from 0 and 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Singularity example (Exercise 4.3.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Σ α_n < ∞ but Σ β_n = ∞ then μ ⟂ ν, showing Σ(α_n − β_n)^2 < ∞ is not sufficient in general for μ ≪ ν.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates necessity of extra hypotheses for the ℓ^2 condition to be sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute continuity via ℓ^1 (Exercise 4.3.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If 0 < α_n, β_n < 1 and Σ |α_n − β_n| < ∞ then μ ≪ ν in general.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An ℓ^1 condition ensures absolute continuity without boundedness away from 0 or 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Branching process martingale and extinction probability (Exercise 4.3.12)
rubrics_metrics.description: For branching process Z_n with offspring generating function φ(θ)=Σ p_k θ^k and ρ ∈ (0,1) solving φ(ρ)=ρ, the process ρ^{Z_n} is a martingale and P(Z_n=0 for some n ≥1 | Z_0=x) = ρ^x.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use martingale property and optional stopping/limit arguments to derive extinction probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doob’s inequality for bounded stopping times (Theorem 4.4.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_n is a submartingale and N is a stopping time with P(N ≤ k) = 1 then E X_0 ≤ E X_N ≤ E X_k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First inequality may fail for unbounded stopping times; proof uses that X_{N∧n} is a submartingale and predictable multipliers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doob’s maximal inequality (Theorem 4.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let X_m be a submartingale, ar X_n = max_{0≤m≤n} X_m^+, λ>0, and A = { ar X_n ≥ λ }. Then λ P(A) ≤ E X_N 1_A ≤ E X_n 1_A ≤ E X_n^+.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take N = inf{m : X_m ≥ λ or m = n}; use Theorem 4.4.1 and the fact X_N ≥ λ on A to bound P(A).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lp maximal inequality (Theorem 4.4.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_n is a submartingale and 1 < p < ∞, then E((ar X_n)^p) ≤ C(p) E((X_n^+)^p) (with an explicit constant depending on p). Consequently for a martingale Y_n and Y^*_n = max_{0≤m≤n} |Y_m|, E|Y^*_n|^p ≤ C(p) E|Y_n|^p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof integrates Doob's inequality, uses Fubini, Lemma 2.2.13, and H�f6lder; typical constant is (p/(p-1))^p/(p-1) up to exact form in the text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kolmogorov's maximal inequality (Example 4.4.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a mean-zero independent-summands random walk S_n with variance var(S_n), P(max_{1≤m≤n} |S_m| ≥ x) ≤ x^{-2} var(S_n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Doob's inequality to X_n = S_n^2 which is a submartingale.

rubrics_metrics.name: No L1 maximal inequality (Example 4.4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general L^1 maximal inequality: a counterexample uses a simple random walk stopped at hitting zero to produce E max_m X_m = ∞ even though EX_n = 1 for all n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows the necessity of p>1 in L^p maximal inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lp convergence theorem (Theorem 4.4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_n is a martingale with sup_n E|X_n|^p < ∞ for p>1, then X_n → X a.s. and in L^p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine martingale convergence theorem (a.s. convergence under uniform integrability-type bounds) with L^p maximal inequality to get boundedness of sup |X_n| in L^p and apply dominated convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthogonality of increments (Theorem 4.4.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_n is a martingale with E X_n^2 < ∞ and m ≤ n and Y ∈ F_m with E Y^2 < ∞ then E((X_n − X_m) Y) = 0; in particular, non-overlapping increments are orthogonal in L^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conditional expectation and the martingale property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional variance formula (Theorem 4.4.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a martingale X_n with E X_n^2 < ∞, E((X_n − X_m)^2 | F_m) = E(X_n^2 | F_m) − X_m^2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditional analogue of var(X) = E X^2 − (E X)^2; proven by expanding square and using conditional expectation linearity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing process for square-integrable martingale (Definition in 4.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For square-integrable martingale X_n (X_0=0, E X_n^2 < ∞), one can decompose X_n^2 = M_n + A_n where A_n = Σ_{m=1}^n E((X_m − X_{m-1})^2 | F_{m-1}). A_n is the increasing process (total pathwise variance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A_n measures accumulated conditional variances; A_∞ = lim A_n is total variance along the path.

rubrics_metrics.name: L2 maximal bound via increasing process (Theorem 4.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: E( sup_{m≤n} |X_m|^2 ) ≤ 4 E A_n. Consequently E( sup_m |X_m|^2 ) ≤ 4 E A_∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the L^2 maximal inequality (Theorem 4.4.4) to obtain this bound; useful for convergence analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergence when total variance finite (Theorem 4.5.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A_∞ < ∞ a.s. then lim_{n→∞} X_n exists and is finite a.s. on {A_∞ < ∞}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Theorem 4.5.1 on stopped processes and L^2 convergence theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growth control via increasing process (Theorem 4.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f ≥ 1 is increasing with ∫_0^∞ f(t)^{-2} dt < ∞, then X_n / f(A_n) → 0 a.s. on {A_∞ = ∞}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct martingale Y_n = Σ (X_m − X_{m-1})/f(A_m) and apply Theorem 4.5.2 and Kronecker's lemma; gives almost sure rate controls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second Borel–Cantelli Lemma, III (Theorem 4.5.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: If B_n is adapted to F_n and p_n = P(B_n | F_{n-1}), then on {Σ p_m = ∞} we have (1/Σ_{m=1}^n p_m) Σ_{m=1}^n 1_{B_m} p_m → 1 a.s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define martingale increments X_n − X_{n-1} = 1_{B_n} − p_n and analyze the associated increasing process; yields a strong form of conditional Borel–Cantelli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedman urn convergence example (Example 4.5.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Friedman�u2019s urn variant (add a balls of drawn color and b of opposite color), starting with g,r>0, the fraction of green balls g_n → 1/2 a.s. under the discussed cases (a=b trivial; a>b and a<b handled via bounds/iteration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Theorem 4.5.5 and martingale arguments applied to counts and proportions to analyze long-run limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: L1/2 bound via increasing process (Theorem 4.5.7)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A refinement of Theorem 4.5.1 using Doob's inequality (Theorem 4.4.2) and integration, giving a better L^1-type bound in terms of sqrt of A_∞.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: uniform integrability (start of 4.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: A family {X_i : i∈I} is uniformly integrable (UI) if lim_{M→∞} sup_{i∈I} E(|X_i| ; |X_i| > M) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UI implies sup_i E|X_i| < ∞; common sufficient condition: domination by an integrable Y (|X_i| ≤ Y, E Y < ∞).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional expectations are UI (Theorem 4.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: For X ∈ L^1 and any sub-σ-field F ⊂ F_0, the collection { E(X | F) : F ⊂ F_0 } is uniformly integrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses dominated convergence and Chebyshev to control tail mass uniformly over σ-fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: UI via Orlicz/Growth function (Theorem 4.6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ ≥ 0 with φ(x)/x → ∞ as x→∞ and E φ(|X_i|) ≤ C uniformly, then {X_i} is uniformly integrable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical choices φ(x)=x^p (p>1) or φ(x)=x log^+ x; proof uses x/φ(x)→0 to bound tails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: UI and L1 convergence (Theorem 4.6.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If E|X_n|<∞ and X_n → X in probability, then (i) {X_n} is UI ⇔ (ii) X_n → X in L^1 ⇔ (iii) E|X_n| → E|X| < ∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard truncation + bounded convergence arguments give equivalences; useful criterion to check L^1 convergence by UI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submartingale UI equivalent to L1 convergence (Theorem 4.6.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a submartingale, UI ⇔ converges a.s. and in L^1 ⇔ converges in L^1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses martingale convergence theorem and Theorem 4.6.3 to connect UI to L^1 and a.s. convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Martingale UI equivalent criteria (Theorem 4.6.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a martingale, the following are equivalent: (i) uniformly integrable, (ii) converges a.s. and in L^1, (iii) converges in L^1, (iv) there exists integrable X with X_n = E(X | F_n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part (iv) characterizes UI martingales as conditional expectations of an integrable limit random variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotone limit of conditional expectations (Theorem 4.6.8)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F_n ↑ F_∞ then E(X | F_n) → E(X | F_∞) a.s. and in L^1 as n→∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Y_n = E(X | F_n) is a martingale; UI (Theorem 4.6.1) gives L^1 convergence and identification of the limit as E(X|F_∞).

rubrics_metrics.name: L�e9vy's 0-1 law (Theorem 4.6.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F_n ↑ F_∞ and A ∈ F_∞ then E(1_A | F_n) → 1_A almost surely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate corollary of Theorem 4.6.8; combined with tail events gives Kolmogorov's 0-1 law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominated convergence for conditional expectations (Theorem 4.6.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Y_n → Y a.s. with |Y_n| ≤ Z where E Z < ∞ and F_n ↑ F_∞, then E(Y_n | F_n) → E(Y | F_∞) a.s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uniform integrability of conditional expectations of W_N = sup_{n,m≥N} |Y_n − Y_m| and Theorem 4.6.8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Backward martingale convergence (Theorem 4.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A backwards martingale X_n (indexed by n ≤ 0, adapted to decreasing σ-fields) satisfies lim_{n→−∞} X_n exists a.s. and in L^1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use upcrossing inequality applied to reversed indexing and uniform integrability from martingale conditional expectation representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit identification for backwards martingale (Theorem 4.7.2)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit lies in tail σ-field and matches conditional expectation on events in F_{−∞}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional expectation monotone limit for decreasing σ-fields (Theorem 4.7.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If F_n ↓ F_{−∞} then E(Y | F_n) → E(Y | F_{−∞}) a.s. and in L^1 as n→−∞.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backward analogue of Theorem 4.6.8; follows from backwards martingale convergence and identification of limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong law via backwards martingales (Example 4.7.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For i.i.d. ξ_i with E|ξ_i| < ∞, S_n/n (indexed backward appropriately) is a backwards martingale; hence S_n/n → E(ξ_1) a.s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates an elegant martingale-based proof of the Strong Law of Large Numbers using backwards martingale convergence and Hewitt–Savage law for triviality of exchangeable tail σ-field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot theorem representation (Example 4.7.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonnegative integer-valued i.i.d. ξ_j and S_k their sums, letting G = {S_j < j for 1≤j≤n}, one has P(G | S_n) = (1 − S_n/n)_+.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proven by constructing backward martingale X_{−j} = S_j/j and optional stopping type argument; gives a conditional probability formula used in ballot theorem applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hewitt–Savage 0-1 law via backwards martingales (Example 4.7.6 and Lemma 4.7.7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_i are i.i.d. and A belongs to the exchangeable σ-field E then P(A) ∈ {0,1}. Lemma 4.7.7 shows empirical symmetrized averages A_n(φ) converge a.s. to E φ(X_1,...,X_k) conditioned on E, and independence arguments force the conditional expectation to be constant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an alternate martingale-based proof of Hewitt–Savage 0-1 law using exchangeability and backward martingale convergence.

rubrics_metrics.name: de Finetti's theorem (Theorem 4.7.9)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_1,X_2,... are exchangeable then conditional on the exchangeable σ-field E the sequence is i.i.d.; i.e., an exchangeable sequence is a mixture of i.i.d. sequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof builds on symmetrized averages and shows factorization of conditional expectations; for {0,1}-valued case this yields representation by an integral over Bernoulli measures (Theorem 4.7.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: de Finetti representation for {0,1}-valued sequences (Theorem 4.7.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X_i ∈ {0,1} are exchangeable then there exists a probability distribution F on [0,1] with P(X_1=1,...,X_k=1,X_{k+1}=0,...,X_n=0) = ∫_0^1 θ^k (1−θ)^{n−k} dF(θ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the classical representation as a mixture of Bernoulli sequences; proofs and quantitative bounds available in referenced literature.
